newsitem.title: USA: Keeping the lid on communications costs.
newsitem.headline: Keeping the lid on communications costs.

text.p: Just when you think you understand your 401(k) plan and you've got control of your mortgage, there's another financial black hole to fall into.
This time it's the high tech-world of communications.

In the new world order of modems, fiber optics and telephone competition, you can get seriously ripped off. Even if all of your services are legit, you may be taking advantage of so many free online services, special cable discounts and long-distance deals that you're haemorrhaging dollars just to stay in touch with the rest of the world.
Consumer groups want to help. This week, the National Consumers League is kicking off a consumer education campaign designed to help people pick and pay for the right services.
Other groups, including Consumer Action and the Telecommunications Research and Action Centre, have published buyers' guides to new phone services.
Before comparison shopping, there are a few rules to know about the communications marketplace.
Rule No. 1: It's constantly changing, and so should you.

Sure, it's a drag to swap your long-distance service every six months, and wouldn't you like your work to be done once you've found your one true Internet connection? Unfortunately, the communications providers are moving targets. The best deal in 1996 may not even be in business in 1997. Even if the companies stay the same, your own communications needs may change.
Hence, Rule No. 2: Start with a budget, so you'll know what you need.

The National Consumers League suggests you create a monthly family communications budget that includes online subscriptions, local and long-distance telephone costs, cable, video rental and pay-per-view bills.

In addition, do a family audit that shows how you use all of those services. When do you make most of your long-distance calls? Are you always dialing the same numbers? What television shows do you really watch?
Armed with that data, you can make intelligent choices.

You may find that you don't watch enough movies to justify a premium cable subscription; you'd do better to rent the movies you watch. A long-distance service that gives you a package on your most dialed numbers might save you money. A pager might suit you better, and be cheaper, than a cellular phone.
And before signing up for service, consider Rule No. 3: Check references.

Many Internet and cellular service providers require a year-long commitment to get their special deals. The last thing you want is to be stuck for a year with a phone that doesn't work or a service provider without adequate service for your call. So don't commit to any communications service unless you've talked to at least one satisfied customer, preferably someone you know.
And now, for some serious sources of comparative communications services:

-- The Telecommunications Research and Action Centre publishes long-distance comparisons every six months for small business and residential consumers. You can get the residential list by sending $3 and a self-adressed, stamped envelope (SASE) to TRAC; P.O. Box 12038; Washington, DC 20005.
-- You can get a survey of prepaid phone cards and their true costs by sending a SASE to Consumers Action Prepaid Phone Cards Survey; 116 New Montgomery Street, Suite 233, San Francisco, CA 94105.

-- If your long-distance bills are so complex, you need a consultant to help you find the best plan, contact the Telecommunications Resellers Association; 1730 K Street, NW., Suite 1201; Washington, DC 20006. They'll recommend an independent agent who can analyse your calls and recommend a low-cost reseller.

-- If you're stumped on how to approach the long-distance question, you can contact the Tele-Consumer Hotline, a non-profit counselling service with English- and Spanish-speaking operators. This project is jointly sponsored by consumer groups and local and long-distance providers. The number is (800) 332-1124.

-- If you're concerned about the risks of online life, including privacy and parental control, you can get information from Project Open, an industry-consumer group project offering assistance on the Web at http://www.isa.net/project-open or on the phone at (800) 466-6736.

You can e-mail Linda Stern at 72160.1546(at)compuserve.com or write to her in care of Reuters; Suite 410, 1333 H St.; NW Washington, DC 20005. She regrets that she cannot answer each letter individually but will cover your questions in upcoming columns.
(EDITORS: Linda Stern is a freelance writer who covers personal finance issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Ms. Stern.)
